Katia

Aliases: 
     Mother Nature, She Who Shapes All  
Race: Human 
Worshippers Race: Mostly humans 
Domains: 
     Air, Animal, Earth, Plant, Water. Clerics of Katia combine the Animal or Plant domains with one of the other domains.
Governs: 
     Nature, forests, agriculture, plants, gardens 


Dogma: 
     Layonara is Nature. Without Nature there is no Layonara; therefore, aid, protect and defend Nature. Oppose those who seek to unbalance Nature. 

Clergy Favored Weapon and Clothing:
     Clerics and Druids of Katia often wear leather armor dyed in green and brown hues, as worked metal makes them feel out of touch with Nature. 

     Followers of Katia usually use large wooden staves, which are actually strong, almost straight straight branches "given" by trees. They also often use longbows. 

Clergy and Temples:
     Katia's dogma is interpretable in many ways, making her faith somewhat individualistic. So, although the clerics and druids of Katia seek to protect and defend Nature, just exactly how this is to be done varies. Despite the differences in interpretation of the dogma, however, the clergy strives to be viewed as a friendly and good faith, since that is more beneficial. There are those who help nature takes its course by nurturing the forests and the plants, planting and nourishing new growth, and helping and nursing sick animals. These are the ones who are generally seen by the populace and have given the Katian faith an aura of good.  

    However, there is more beneath the surface than meets the eye. There are also those who believe that Nature cannot survive without their help. Civilization is spreading across Layonara and is proving a threat to its wilderness. Already, the forest that once covered Mistone completely has been severed into forests of a smaller size such as the Silkwood, the Whitehorn Forest, and the Gloom Woods. Roads have been laid across the wild plains and agricultural fields spread every year to feed the mouths of those who live in the ever-expanding cities.

     These more extreme followers of Katia will use drastic measures to prevent the felling of the forests, the cultivation of the plains, and the expansion of the cities. They will not shy from breeding fierce animals and setting them loose in order to make areas less safe and prevent villages from expanding. They will also not shy from covertly sponsoring bands of brigands to frequent certain areas, making roads less passable and allowing them to be grown over again.

     However, regardless of how a follower of Katia interprets the dogma, they realize that everything involving Nature takes time and planning. It might take years for their plans to bear fruit, just as it takes years for a sapling to become a tree.

     Because of Katia's dogma being subject to interpretation, there is not one Church of Katia. Followers are loosely organized and tend to live in small groups, with each group being headed by its most senior member. There is no strong, central hierarchy.

     Temples to Katia cannot be found in cities, but are groves secreted away deep in the forests, or large standing stones at the edges of forests.

     Clerics of Katia pray for their spells at sunrise. Prayers to Katia usually involve terminology referencing Nature, like plants, animals, or weather.

     Special holy days are the first days of spring, summer, autumn, and winter.

Baraeon Ca'duz

Aliases: Prince of Hate, Lord of Spiders, Left Hand of Black  
Race: Dark Elf 
Worshippers: Dark Elf males only
Domains: Death, Evil, Trickery
Governs: Hatred, revenge, cruelty, spiders, darkness 
 
     Baraeon was the dark elven hero that led his people into the darkness after they were betrayed by the other elven clans. 
     Baraeon taught his people how to live in the darkness, and with the help of Pyrtechon the race of dark elves thrived. Baraeon also taught his people the arts of revenge and cruelty. 
His own personal revenge against the surface elves culminated when he poisoned the first born daughter of Ilsare. Taking the form of a spider, he managed to sneak into the Ilsare's chambers, where she slept with her young child. Baraeon poisoned the child, and then woke Ilsare so she could watch the child die in her arms. Pyrtechon rewarded Baraeon by elevating him to godhood. 

Dogma: 
     Vengeance is an art. It is sweet and should be savored, a pleasure not to be rushed. Nothing is more satisfying than watching your plans for revenge come to fruition and have the object of your retribution realize you were behind it...but realize too late. The Prince of Hate will look down favorably upon you if your subterfuge remains hidden to all but your target. The weak and the faithless should be destroyed. 

     Dark elves are the supreme race, and Dark Elf males are better than females. 

     The Dark Elves shall reign supreme in Underdark. Annihilate the surface elves and take their lands from them. Do not aid the enemies of the People. Strive to better yourselves, even at the expense of others; this way you will gain and keep the power that is rightfully yours. Do not harm any spider, ever. Harming a spider is an affront to Baraeon Ca'Duz, and should only be done if the spider's poison is used for the art of vengeance.

Clergy Favored Weapon and Clothing:
     Priests of Baraeon Ca'Duz prefer to use a shortsword slathered with poisons. Their garb is predominantly black, and stained with dark shades of green. Around their neck they wear a medallion in the shape of a spider, the symbol of their god. 

Clergy and Temples:
     Priests of Baraeon Ca'Duz are the most powerful people in Dark Elf society, next to Priestesses of Vierdri'ira. Every Dark Elf city has one temple for the Prince of Hate. Temples are led by a High Priest, who only remains in that rank as long as no craftier or more powerful Priest removes him from that position.

     Temples to the Lord of Spiders are usually shaped like a spider. One enters a Temple through one of the legs, immediately noticing the greenish light that permeates the entire temple. Depending on the size of the temple, four legs are for training the male clerics. One leg is home to the acolytes' quarters, and one is home to the high clergy. 

     The central body of the spider is the Hall of Poisons. This Hall is filled with webs and spiders, and it is here that the general worship of Baraeon Ca'Duz takes place. The head of the spider is the Inner Sanctum, where the most profane rituals are performed and the temple's treasure and relics are housed. Only the eight highest clerics are authorized to or capable of entering the Sanctum.

     Females are not allowed to enter temples of the Left Hand of Black, on pain of death. This was not the case until about 1500 years ago, when Az'atta betrayed Baraeon Ca'Duz.  Until then, both males and females worshipped the Prince of Hate. However, after being betrayed by Az'atta, Baraeon had his male followers expel or kill all of his female clerics as an act of vengeance for Az'atta's betrayal.

     Males who do not worship Baraeon Ca'Duz but enter the Inner Sanctum are to be sought out and killed unless they are converted to worship Baraeon within 7 days. Proof of conversion is given by undergoing the Test - the same set of trials all Dark Elves have to go through to prove their loyalty to their deities and their People - to demonstrate their loyalty to Vierdri'ira and Baraeon; those who fail either die or are transformed into the fearsome Driders. 

     Clerics pray for their spells before they go into reverie. Prayers are often couched with references to spiders, webs, and poison: "Lord of Spiders, grant me your favor that my enemies do not notice the web of intrigue I have spun to ensure their demise."

Mistone
    Mistone is a continent in the western part of the hemisphere. It seems to be one of the few places which have not yet felt the crushing impact of Bloodstone's most recent wave of invasions, though most believe this dread will come in time. The reason for this relative isolation is that Mistone has for many years now been semi-autonomous. Although Mistone is of course still under the rule of Dregar and the capital of Prantz, this remote influence is not often felt. More likely if you ask a Mistoner who rules, they will tell you Queen Allurial in Blackford Castle. Mistone has remained relatively stable in terms of economic infrastructure, a large factor in its relative self-sufficiency. Lately this illusory sovereignty is being seen with increasing frequency and intensity to be just that, an illusion. Some attribute this to unchecked growth. Others believe it is the effect of more sinister machinations.

Well-known Cities:

Hlint
Location 
    Hlint lies close to the center of the continent of Mistone. 
Population 
    1,830 (60% Human, 15% Halfling, 10% Dwarf, 5% Half-Orc, 5% Gnome, 5% Elf) 
Government:  Monarchy 
Defenses:
    There are wooden walls within and around parts of this city. They are mostly decorative, however, or used to partition space within the town itself. For protection, the denizens of Hlint primarily rely on Fort Llast, their neighbors to the west.

Miscellaneous Information:
    Hlint is a boom town. Of course, it is neither as grand as Leilon to the northwest nor as established as Fort Llast to the west. Nevertheless, it has grown in just about every aspect due to several clear reasons. Hlint fortuitously lies on unarguably the most secure and therefore most traveled east-west passage on the continent of Mistone. On the north side of this well-trodden road are the Greypeak Mountians, and the Silkwood Forest grows to the south. Both the mountains and the woods beckon to would-be adventurers and resource seekers, bringing them in droves from all over the continent. Because of this, Hlint has become the adopted home of most of those who call themselves adventurers on the continent of Mistone. Some of the great heroes of our age have made roots in this bustling town and The High Council of Layonara has made Hlint its headquarters. This also means that Hlint has been the stage for countless dramas, some universal, some inane, and some far reaching in their global sociopolitical ramifications. A temple of Ilsare can be found here as well.

Leilon
Location: 
    Leilon is situated in the northwest corner of the continent of Mistone. 
Population:
    3,575 (50% human, 30% half-orc, 12% halfling, 3% dwarf, 3% gnome, 2% elf) 
Government:  Monarchy 
Defenses:  
    Leilon is well defended by thick stone walls which climb over twenty feet in most places. Along the top of the walls are ramps and embattlements.

Miscellaneous Information:
    The city of Leilon began as a small town some 300 years ago. The inhabitants were people who migrated away from the thriving cities the south looking for their own niche on the continent of Mistone. For approximately the first one hundred years of their existance, life was fairly serene and prosperous. The population of the town grew, and began to attract more artisans and scholarly types.

    Unfortunately it was around that time that the barbarian tribes of the north discovered Leilon. The tribe called the Long Axes raided the town, decimated the male population, and left many women raped and with child. The Long Axes filled their longboats with loot, leaving the town with little food for the winter. Many of the people fled to the south, and the town's population dwindled from over 10,000 to a mere 2,000. The harsh winter further whittled the population down to less than 1,000. That spring the people rebuilt their town and prosperity soon returned. Life appeared to have returned to normal, until the Long Axes returned in the fall. The Long Axes would have destroyed the village for good, but for a retired old mage named Arn of Corbone. He had come to the village in the summer, looking for a place to spend the last of his years. The news of the raid last fall almost made him leave again, but his old body was in need of rest after weeks of travel. Arn expected the Long Axes to return that winter. With great effort and skill, he managed to rally the town, organize the defenses, and quell the barbarian assault. The barbarians would not return for several years after their encounter with Arn.

    The Long Axes were fierce warriors, acustomed to fighting. When they returned that fall, they smashed their way through the defenses and proceeded to raid the town as they had before. Taking matters into his own hands, Arn called upon his considerable magic powers, and changed the history of both Leilon and the Long Axe tribe. Many of the Long Axe warriors fell to the firestorms that erupted from Arn's fingers. Arn was ruthless, mowing down Long Axe warriors as they fled back to their longboats. Fearing that his tribe would be destroyed, Ingmar Stormhammer, the Long Axe chief, sacrificed himself in what many still regard an epic battle. Ingmar leapt through a wall of flames, and drove his spear through the chest of an incredulous Arn of Corbone, who did not even try to get out of the way. The flames had left Ingmar mortally wounded as well. The few remaining Long Axe warriors limped home in their longboats. The catastrophe at Leilon ultimately forced the Long Axes to be absorbed by other tribes.

    The winter passed with little incident. That spring, an old friend of Arn's came to Leilon to visit. His name was Golvin Dawntella, a knight of the Griffin. The people greeted him warmly, and several townsfolk asked him to make the town his demesne. While Golvin was saddened by the loss of his friend, he was also intrigued by the opportunity of becoming the town's leader. Golvin sent for his retainers, and gave his old lands to his younger brother. Golvin then asked the mayor for his daughter's hand in marriage to further cement his claim on the town of Leilon.

    Golvin set about building his keep and organizing the town's militia. Over the next five years, the town prospered greatly. The keep was completed, and a wall was erected around the town. The militia was formed and trained. The town was well prepared when a coalition of barbarian tribes attacked that fall. The militia was outnumbered six to one, but were able to barely repel the raid.

    The battle inspired what would eventually be a war between Leilon and the barbarians to the north for the next 80 years. Over the years the Leilon Militia established themselves as one of the best on all of Mistone. The barbarians did have several victories, but as the years wore on, the militia established themselves as superior. Eventually, the barbarians gave up trying to sack what was now the city of Leilon.

    Since that time, relations with the barbarians have steadily improved, and now the two factions are very good trading partners. With no enemies to fight, the city of Leilon has since focused itself into becoming a major trading power. The discovery of whaling some forty years ago only contributes to what was already a booming economy.

    There are some on the continent of Mistone who would, if asked, point to the city of Leilon as an example of the brutal aftermath of a leader installed by military necessity. For in Leilon, justice is said to be as swift as the coin flows. Poverty and wealth seem to grow hand in hand. Yet none dare challenge the Blackwatchers, the Leilon city guard, who follow orders with ruthless efficiency.

    A temple of Mist can be found in Leilon.

Melar
Location:

Population:
800 (40% human, 20% halfling, 15% elf, 15% gnome, 5% half-orc, % dwarf) 
Government: 
    Melar is organized as a feudal city-state subordinated to the nearby Blackford Castle.

    Melar has traditionally been the starting point for most expeditions heading beyond the lower range of the Hammerbound Peaks. Center
Location:  As the name suggests, Center is located in the center of the continent of Mistone.
Population:
3400 (50% Human, 22% Halfling, 18% Dwarf, 10% Elf)
Government:  Center is ruled by a council of merchants.
Defenses: A small wall surrounds the town.

Far Reach
Location:  Far Reach is on the western side of the continent of Mistone, west of the Silkwood and North of Forest of Moans.

Fort Hope
Location:  Fort Hope is centrally located on the island of Mistone, just south of the Broken Forest
Population: 760
Government:  
    Fort Hope has a two-tier system of government. There is a military commander to run the Fort's garrisons and military function as well as an appointed mayor who administers the social and economic affairs of the fort.

Defenses:  
    An old and resilient military outpost, Fort Hope is well defended.

Miscellaneous Information:
    The first thing you'll likely notice upon entering this centrally located Mistone outpost are the tents, caravans and newly built structures. These new developments arise in the wake of recent migration to the area. For years Fort Hope served as a watch station for the undead, which often overflowed from the Broken Forest. This fact made Fort Hope one of the least desirable posts on the continent. This is true particularly since clean-up crews frequently left the safety of the fort to remove the walking rot and shadows from the crucial road which runs north and south through the forest. These crews almost never returned. And for hundreds of years the road remained hopelessly overrun, controlled by some unknown sinister influence.
The optimistic name of this post has always seemed to play with this kind of historic irony. Although many believe the name of the fort derived from the hope to curtail the evil influence of the Broken Forest, more investigation will reveal that it was actually established and named during the race wars.
A small group of humans pushed past the front lines, situated on the then sublime forest, and supplanted an elven outpost in that same location. Once the fort was captured, their only hope for survival and victory was the drive of the great human general Draislar. He was to wedge through the elven armies of the Far Reach plains and the Broken Forest to regroup at the fort and use it as a base of operations. Draislar never arrived. The battle which ensued claimed the lives of Draislar and his army, but also, and quite mysteriously, the bulk of the elven armies of the region. This battle marked the beginning of the end of the elf and human wars on Mistone. And with countless souls strewn upon the desecrated forest floor, the human chapter of Far Reach began.
The most recent and most prosperous chapter of Fort Hope's history begins with the heroic deeds of the rangers Triba Guess and Enzo Reynolt, who mended the long broken nature of the forest. Once the dead no longer rose to torment the living, the road north and south became passable and the frequency of caravans looking for a respite at the Fort increased rapidly. Fort Hope is coming into its own as a key security and mercantile force, made more crucial by its central location and resilient traditions.

Forewarn Fort 
Location:  
    Fort Forewarn is on the eastern shores of the continent of Mistone. 
Population: 
4,000 (45% human, 20% halfling, 15% half-orc, 10% dwarf, 15% gnome, 5% elf) 
Government:  Feudalism 
Defenses:
    Masonry walls surround this city. The walls are reinforced for protection from attacks from the sea.

Miscellaneous Information: 
    This is a primary shipping port between the continent of Mistone and Dregar. As such, Forewarn Fort is a major inlet of goods and information as well as a good place to leave Mistone in the aft horizon. With good shipping routes, however, come pirates. The Gulf of Bagira to the north of Forewarn is known to be a pirate hideout and launching point. With the Forsaken Islands off the coast, and stories of whole ships becoming marauding crews of undead, only pirates or fools would sail those waters. These facts draw the seedy elements of Mistone to Forewarn, making it a rough town as well as a sound choice for the headquarters of the Mistone Alliance.

Fort Llast
Location:  
    Fort Llast is in the northwestern part of Mistone. It can be found on the east-west road that runs through Hlint and meets up with the road that runs north and south between Blackford Castle and Krandor.
Population:  275
Government:  
    The government in Fort Llast is a strict military hierarchy under the command of Lieutenant Jursen who answers to Blackford Castle.
Defenses:  
    There is a short stone wall surrounding the city. It is also home to a Temple of Toran, so there are always a couple of paladins around.

Miscellaneous Information:
    A quick glance at a map of Mistone can tell the story of this town's significance. The fort lies at the crossroads of two of the most frequented roads on the continent. This allows the Llast guards to monitor most of the travel and trading in northern Mistone. It is also the job of the Fort to ensure the road which connects Leilon, Blackford Castle and Port Hempstead far to the south remains open and relatively safe. When Fort Llast is well staffed, and it almost always is, guards can be found patrolling the road as far south as the Broken Forest and north until it reaches the ocean at Leilon. 
Monitoring and ensuring smooth movement on Mistone, however, are secondary considerations. Fort Llast was founded in a warm summer of the early 3rd century, at the height of the Human and Elf wars. Blackford Castle was the seat of human power on the continent even then. In the 287th year after the Cataclysm, the castle nearly fell to the elves, an outcome which could have altered the fate of humans and elves on Mistone. 

    Despite being heavily garrisoned and defended, the castle was caught unprepared by the waves of elves who seemed to appear on the Grunwald Plains as swiftly as an ocean storm. Peasants, merchants and guards carrying crucial supplies scrambled to reach the castle before the portcullis fell. Many were left stranded outside and were slaughtered by a hailstorm of elven arrows and bolts. Startled and dismayed by the grisly scene just beyond the walls, the humans who did make it to the castle struggled to regain composure and perform their duties. The disciplined Blackford soldiers, however, snapped into action with drilled precision and managed to turn back wave after wave of elf invaders. 
The elves, however, came prepared to smother every human in that castle with fear and hunger. Their numbers were great, and swelled even greater with reinforcements after each skirmish. The blockade was complete. So with every human soldier pinned in the castle and the nearest garrison far to the south with no hope of contact, the castle lay under siege for months. It took that long before the humans, with the help of some dwarf miners caught in the outskirts, tunneled beneath the castle to a small valley in the Hammerbound Peaks. There, two small groups of scouts emerged. One made the trek to Leilon, where they sailed south to the Rodilin Hills to alert the marauding human armies. The second traversed the treacherous peaks to call upon the aid of Haven Castle.

    The elves, pinched by a human army moving north along the Zainge River and another moving west along the northern border of Silkwood forest, were forced to retreat. Elves flowed into the Silkwood and vanished among the ancient trees. At that moment it was clear that the elves had used the cover of the forest to amass their armies and establish supply lines. Thus, Fort Llast was built, perfectly situated as a first line of defense against elven invasion from the deep shadows of the Silkwood forest.

Fort Vehl
Location: 
    Fort Vehl lies at the very southern tip of Mistone between the Battlehelm Moors and the southern ranges of the Brech Mountians.
Population: 9385
Government:  
    Fort Vehl is ruled by an allegedly corrupt military dictator.
Defenses:  
    Thick stone walls and battlements surround the city to protect it from terrestrial attacks. However, the town's defenses are more oriented toward guarding the crucial docks.

Miscellaneous Information:
    At the southernmost part of the continent, Fort Vehl is the primary point of connection between Mistone and Rilara. Port Hempstead is the place for more official dockings, but anyone who knows anything about Rilara will know that is why Velensk prospers. In contrast to Port Hempstead, the relative isolation of Fort Vehl between the Brech Mountainsto the east and the Battlehelm Moors to the west, as well as having no significant settlements nearby, makes it a preferred destination for more nefarious Rilaran traffic. The large and defensible docks contribute to this function as well. In Rilara, Milara's dominion is said to be total. And considering his grasping ambition, particularly his goal to bring all of Mistone under his sway, Fort Vehl is busy indeed.

    With this said, it is obvious that the fort is a wickedly volatile place. The economic and political elite barely attempt to maintain a thin veil of respectability, a veil which only ever fools the most vapid or gormless transients. Many residents live in squalor; they dwell in alleys and sewers, feeding off of the shipping rubbish and dockside rats. Pirates and outlaws and Rilaran agents of disruption flow through the city with seeming impunity. Of course, this is only true so long as such unseemly agents do not counter the direct interests of the ruling elite. With such desperate and corruptible characters in force on its streets, Fort Vehl also proves an ideal headquarters for mercenary recruiters. Equally logical is the presence of the temple of Rofirien, which beams light from its shimmering surfaces over the dark streets. It is one of the few places of mercy in Mistone's most notorious den of villainy. The men who vault their essence in the Fort Vehl temple and undertake Rofirien's mission of justice are compelled by unmatched faith, often deadly but always selfless. They are among Mistone's most valorous.

Haven
Location:  
    Haven can be found on the eastern rim of Mistone.
Population:  3,300 (50% humans, 30% dwarves, 10% halflings, 10% elves)
Government:  
    Monarchy with landed serfs in surrounding areas
Defenses:  
    The outskirts of Haven, where most reside, are not defended except for by foot patrols. If the town is raided, as many as possible are pulled into the heavily defended stone walls of the castle.

Miscellaneous Information:
    Haven is most noted for the trade route it was built upon. Forewarn Fort, which ships the majority of the continent's goods, is just to the south and Haven is directly between it and the capital of Blackford. Also, while the route is longer, it is still safer for the convoys from Port Hempstead to head through the city rather then the often treacherous forest.

    For many centuries the people of Mistone traveled this long stretch of road with nothing but their own blades to defend the goods they rode with. Eventually small towns began to sprout, offering travelers some refuge from bandits as well as the harsh seasonal weather. 

    These towns brought much relief and grew quickly as the valuable goods stopped in their markets before heading off to their ultimate destination. As the settlements grew, they became all the more ripe for any man brave enough to take advantage of their actual weaknesses. Milick was such a man. 

    Milick was an intelligent man who felt stifled and oppressed by the huge merchant conglomerates of the city. Angered by this, he decided to exact revenge. Milick organized a convoy that would follow the normal route north at the same time as many other convoys. That way, they would all stop near the same locations during the night. Of course, instead of goods, he was carrying a small army of mercenaries bought from the streets of the city. As the other convoys slept under cover of the small towns, Milick's men raided them, killing guards and merchants in their sleep and stealing the goods for themselves. 
Milick ran northwest with his men and booty, hoping to camp within the forest. There he would gather more men and fence his stolen goods to increase the numbers and quality of his army for hire. His desire for vengeance upon Haven could not be assuaged. 

    During the night a fight broke out between Milick and his own appointed mercenary captain. They quarreled over whether they should continue the plan or just settle with the money they had. Angered by the change of plans, Milick lunged at the captain and ripped him open with his blade before the mercenaries could subdue him. By the time they had finished, he had been beaten to death. The next day, they returned to the fort only to find the peasants of the Haven fields rallied and fervent about blocking the hired army's path. A fierce battle ensued, but the peasants eventually managed to overcome the mercenaries, who underestimated the determination of the farmers as well as the sharpness of their scythes. With the captured gold and goods, these unlikely heroes set about creating the fort so travelers and locals could find reliable shelter in dire times.

Krandor
Location:  
    In the central western part of Mistone.
Population: 1600 (60% human, 30% elf, 10% Halfling)
Government:  
    Krandor has a mayor, chosen by the property-owning families in the vicinity.
Defenses:  The only defense Krandor has is a few patrolling guards.

Miscellaneous Information:
    Where the western edge of the Silkwood forest dances endlessly with the expansive meadows just beyond lies the town of Krandor. The unobtrusive architecture and lack of clear border make Krandor seem in harmony with the natural landscape. Because of this, many outdoorsmen are drawn to this town. Some go to Krandor to use the town as a launching point for hunting expeditions into the Silkwood. Others fall in love with the forest and attempt to halt, or at least try to manage the impact such groups have upon the forest. 

Lar
Location: Near the Highstar lake in the Hammerbound Peaks.
Population: 1200
Government: Feudalism
Defenses: 
    Lar can only be reached by a narrow mountain trail, which can be easily defended by just a handful of guards. 

Miscellaneous Information:
    Lar is very small and remote. It's more of a trader's outpost than a town. Most of those who call Lar home serve the miners and trappers who live and wander in the Hammerbound Peaks. Locals speak of the town being founded on the banks of a gorgeous mountain waterfall by Larnida. In recent years, a statue has been erected on that spot to commemorate the event. On founder's day, and other somewhat secretive ritual days, people bring offerings to the statue. 

    There are many dwarves in Lar. This is either a fortuitous circumstance for defense against the many giant attacks upon the city, or the dwarves have come to Lar for a piece of the action. As a trading outpost for trappers and miners, with a high dwarven population and unceasing attacks from giants, life in Lar is clearly a demanding and arduous endeavor. That's why those who call Lar home are some of the most gruff and resilient people to be found on all of Mistone. Lar is also the village where Ta'karsh Blacklung, High Hammer of Dorand, has chosen to build the Citadel of the Hammer in honor of Dorand, god of crafters.

List
Location:  
    List is southwest of the High Moor swamp on the continent of Mistone, near Haven Castle.
Population:
1,175 (45% human, 20% half-orc, 15% dwarf, 10% halfling, 5% gnome, 5% elf) 
Government:  Feudalism 
Defenses:
    List is without defenses.

Miscellaneous Information:
    List is affiliated, both economically and politically, with Haven Castle to the southeast. It is little more than a center for the widely dispersed farmers of the area to come for company, supplies, and transport to the Haven markets for their goods. As such, the residents of the town proper are far outnumbered by those living in the outlying agricultural areas.

Liken
Location:  
    Liken is found at the coast of the northeast corner of the continent of Mistone.
Population:  360
Government:  Chiefdom
Defenses:  
    Liken has no defenses.

Miscellaneous Information:
    Nestled in the coastal hills of northeast Mistone and blessed with the perfect climate for growing pipeweed, Liken is a popular place for halflings. There is a single dock right in the middle of the town which launches and receives small ships for local distribution of Liken's and the northeast region's goods.

Kheldell
Location: 
    Kheldell is on the northern tip of Mistone in the Whitehorn Forest.
Population:
350 (60% human, 20% elf, 5% halfling, 5% dwarf, 5% gnome, 5% half-orc) 
Government:  Theocracy
Defenses: 
    A wooden palisade surrounds this small hamlet. 

Miscellaneous Information:
    Kheldell is a somewhat self-sufficient town located where the High and Lost Forests together meet the ocean. The town is a part of the forest, obtaining every resource for nourishment, warmth, and shelter from the verdant woodland. As such, Kheldell's residents are raised to be resilient, surviving cycles of intense hardship. The woodsmen who take to this arduous lifestyle are proud of the town and its accomplishments. They therefore tend to discourage outsiders from doing anything more than passing through. They discourage all hopeful settlers except the occasional individual bearing the unmistakably weathered signs of a rugged past spent working the woods. The docks, used sparingly and typically to import regional goods from Liken, are closed to outsiders without prior authorization except, of course, in cases of emergency.

Krelin's Tents 
Location: 
    In the Blood Desert on the continent of Mistone 
Population:
120 (60% human, 25% half-orc, 10% halfling, 2% gnome, 2% dwarf, 1% elf) 
Government:  Tribal 
Defenses:  None 

Miscellaneous Information:
    This is a good resting spot when traveling in the Blood desert. It is virtually the only water available for nearly 100 miles. 

Port Hempstead
Location:  
    Port Hempstead is the major city and port on the southwest coast of the continent of Mistone. 
Population: 
49,000 (70% human, 15% halfling, 5% dwarf, 4% gnome, 4% elf, 2% half-orc) 
Government:  Feudalism 
Defenses: 
    Superior masonry walls surround much of the city. In some key places the walls are also reinforced. In addition to this, some of the walls have also been magically reinforced. 

Miscellaneous Information: 
    This city is rich and prosperous. Large veins of gold and silver are shipped in from the Ire Mountains to the northeast. If an adventurer is looking for something special, she is likely to find it in this city.
Six hundred years ago, this great city was destroyed by a combined force of Drow and dragons. The city was left shattered and stripped as the forces plundered over five million gold from it. The city struggled to rebuild, as the Duke had lost his former power and its resources had been plundered. The only sources of capital in the wake of the destruction were the individual merchants. They pulled together and as quickly as they could began rebuilding the city and raising armies. Their interest in the port and their links to the invaluable resources in the surrounding areas were dear enough to risk everything to defend it. 
The Duke, still attempting to retain authority, could do little to stop the organized merchants.  On several occasions when he attempted to defy them, the merchants quickly placed him under house arrest and kept his castle guarded at all times by their own superior troops, effectively making him a puppet. For centuries this arrangement persisted, and the Dukes of each successive generation increasingly came to accept their fate as adjuncts of the city economy. Every attempt to act otherwise was swiftly curtailed. Now the Duke's tradition in Port Hempstead is to work for and within the systems of power established by the merchants. Through this arrangement, the merchant organizations and the Duke have merged interests and formed a coherent power structure.

    The bottom line in Port Hempstead is still an economic one. The peasants and landowners who live in the surrounding areas often complain about being under the boot of the Port. The laws of the land are implemented to protect the interests of the major merchant powers, who sometimes use this fact to expand their exploitative labor practices and resource capturing endeavors. Some say this is the cause of the unrest which has emerged in the southwest region. Others believe the uprising it is not a legitimate grass roots movement in the interests of those in the shadow of the port, but a machination implemented by Milara or demons or both to destabilize the region in preparation for future maneuvers. Some believe it is both.
Major Temples of Deliar and Shadon can be found in Port Hempstead.

Brenuth
Location:
    Southern part of the continent of Mistone, right in the middle of the Brech Mountains. 
Population: 
6,500 (85% Mountain Dwarf, 5% halfling, 5% human, 3% gnome, 1% elf, 1% half-orc) 
Government: Monarchy 
Defenses: 
    This Dwarven city is surrounded by superior masonry walls that are further reinforced with fiercely guarded Dwarven skills passed on through oral tradition.

Miscellaneous Information:
    Brenuth, also called Gem of Brech, is a very proud city steeped in tradition. They do not like outsiders and only after years of living among them will one be grudgingly accepted. This only ever happens when an individual works through the labor and crafting ranks, all the while supporting and defending the community. 
The majority of the populace are devout followers of Dorand and Vorax, and the arms and armors created by the Brenuth smithies are of great renown.

Vorax

Aliases: The Father of Battle, The Eternally Vigilant  
Race: Dwarf 
Worshippers: Primarily worshipped by dwarves. Although strong warriors of other races (especially human) will often times call upon the Father of Battle as well. 
Domains: Good, War, Protection 
Governs: Battle, war, valor, bravery, vigilance 

Dogma:
     Vorax honors all who believe in bravery, war and valor. His clerics despise weakness of character, believing one should have strong moral values. They hate pacifism, as any morals and ideals worth having should also be worth fighting for. They loathe an idle mind, as it becomes fertile ground for unrighteous seeds to plant themselves, and equally hate an idle body, as it becomes soft and unsuitable for the rigors of war. They have a great mistrust of arcane magics, and as a result generally do not mix well with wizards and other arcane spell-casters. Above all, the clerics of Vorax abhor dishonorable and deceitful tricksters. War should be fought for righteous causes, and won through honorable battle. 

     War is a sacred rite for the followers of Vorax, and as such is never entered into lightly. War should always be an option of last resort and should only be engaged in for the most just of causes. However, once engaged, a war should be fought strictly by the established rules and the righteous cause must be made victorious. There is no shame in losing a battle, but there is great dishonor in losing a war. To lose a war is to fail the just and the righteous, and therefore show weakness in the Father of Battle. Because war is so sacred to the church, the tools of war are considered sacred instruments. Thus, weapons of war are treated with great reverence. 

     To encompass all of this, a follower of Vorax must have a strong and just moral character. Followers of Vorax must be like The Ever Vigilant himself, keeping their bodies and minds prepared at all times to defend the just and righteous of the world. 

Clergy Favored Weapon and Clothing: 
     The favored weapon of the clergy of Vorax is the battleaxe, although many of the dwarven clergy prefer the dwarven variety. Silvered varieties of weapons are often favored as well, as they are exceptionally handy when fighting the undead minions of one of Vorax's biggest enemies, Corath. 

     The favored armor of the clergy and followers is strong, hardy full plate, often painted in silver and red to emulate the armor worn by Vorax himself. The temple clergy rarely wear such armor, but they do still possess it. Instead, temple clergy tend to wear robes of red or black with silver and gold highlights and threading. They tend to wear very formal robes, however, since such attire is less conducive to idleness of the body. Battle Priests of Vorax rarely go anywhere without their armor on. Instead, they have robes fitted to be worn over the outside of their armor. Although most followers actually spend less time in armor than without, the Battle Priests are the exception, usually only taking it off to sleep, bathe, or clean the armor itself. 

Clergy and Temples: 
     The hierarchy of the church of Vorax is broken down into three divisions, each with its own way of doing things. 

     The first sect is the Scholar Clerics of Vorax. These are by far the most numerous as they are often educators and counselors of the lay as well as the devout. These clerics are the ones who rely on prayer as much as anything else as a daily guide in their lives. This sect is led by a council of elders, who in turn give authority to carry forth the word to other members of their order as they see fit. Only the most pious and devout followers of Vorax ever sit on the council. Once there, they sit for life; only when a member dies will another be chosen to fill his or her place. This new member is chosen by secret ballot by the council. The ballots are kept secret as to prevent clan rivalry from influencing votes. The longest-sitting member of the council is the leader, holding the title of High Elder of Vorax. 

     The second sect is the Battle Priests of Vorax. These priests spend less time in communal prayer with Vorax, and as such do not wield his power as fully as those of the scholarly sect. What they lack in divine strength, however, they make up for in strength of arms. Unlike their scholarly counterparts, Battle Priests spend more time honing their bodies and minds for war than they do in pious contemplation. Many of the strongest warriors of the time can be found among the Battle Priests, but raw strength alone does not suit them; Battle Priests must also be wise in the ways of war. Battle Priests often become generals of armies and leaders of men, for through long and intensive study and actual field practice, they have learned the intricacies of battle strategy and the true art of war. No Battle Priest begins in the sect; rather, they are called to it over time. Sometimes a scholar finds within their studies a calling to become more like Vorax, and so takes up arms and begins fighting more and praying less. Other times grizzled warriors begin to learn that there is more to war than brute force, and begin to study its art and learn more of Vorax, that they may find his favor come time for battle. The hierarchy of the Battle Priests is rigid. All Battle Priests have a standing within the hierarchy which they are made to memorize from top to bottom so that there is never a question of whose authority is greater. The very top of the hierarchy is the General Superior of Vorax. The General Superior is the longest standing member of the Council of Battle Generals. There are seven Generals, each of equal rank, and all others fall below them. Promotion through the ranks for those below them can only happen in two ways, either there is a death, and everyone moves up, or the Generals promote one of those they lead to a higher position. Only the General Superior can promote a Battle Priest to the elevated position of Battle General of Vorax. The Battle Generals of Vorax are the most capable warleaders to be found anywhere. 

     The third sect of the church is the Order of the Bloody Axe. These clergy are also militant, but are in the service of either of the previous sects. They have the divine strength granted to them through close communing with Vorax, but the strength of body of a warrior or Battle Priest. These are the Paladins of Vorax, and in some rare cases Champions of Vorax. The hierarchy here is very loose. Once a person is accepted as a Paladin of Vorax, it is expected that they need no hierarchy to give them guidance or structure. They are glowing beacons of good and righteous character with unimpeachable moral fiber. Among their kind, though, there is a certain amount of deference for those that have served longer as Paladins, for the longer they have served, the more experience eradicating evil they have had. There is but one elevated position among the given to its longest standing member: the Righteous Axe of Vorax.

     Although rarely ever assembled, the leaders of each of the three sects form the High Council of Vorax. It is these three that come together in times of crisis to provide direction for the church, and it is this council of three that has final say in the interpretation of church doctrine and mission. It is also this council that, on very rare occurrences, will select from among the followers a Champion of Vorax. This Champion nearly always comes from the Battle Priests or the Paladins, and serves as an honorary member of the High Council of Vorax until death. 

     Prayer times for each of the sects vary. Scholars pray quite frequently throughout the day, praying as they rise from their rest at dawn and again at the end of the day before retiring for the night, at a minimum. They also offer prayer after any intervention by Vorax is perceived, such as after a healing is performed or a battle won. Battle Priests pray far less often, since they rely as much on their own ability as the intervention of Vorax. They do acknowledge Vorax at the beginning of each day, and always before engaging in planned battle. The prayer practices of Paladins are much like those of Battle Priests, but they will pray for guidance and strength at any time they feel that their services will be needed to ensure that Vorax helps them in their righteous cause. 

     The only religious holiday observed by the church as a whole is the first day of the new year. It is held in reverence as a reminder of the rebirth and reaffirmation of good and life in the world. As to other days of celebration and revelry, they are usually clan-based and used to mark the day of some great battle in the history of the clan.

Blackfeather Mountains
    The Blackfeather Mountains sit just north of the forest of Fog. Years ago the Broken Glade Giants drove out the hordes of crows that settled in the eastern parts of the forest. No one is sure why the crows were there or why the Giants drove them out, but after they flapped wildly around the forest for a week or so they came to rest on the mountains just to the north. If you walk through one of the long abandoned dwarf trails through these peaks you'll find layers of crow's feathers at your feet. Despite the slippery footing, it is still worth the treacherous walk. The views of the forest, desert and ocean from even the lower ranges are breathtaking.

Black Hills
    When you are in the Black Hills you'll know it. The soil here is jet black and seems to radiate an unnatural darkness. Even on a cloudless summer's noon, the hills seem dimmed. These dark, foreboding mounds can be seen from a distance. Most people are thankful for this, as they become easier to avoid. Despite the many roads which wind their way through these hills, travelers are seldom seen.
    If you do venture to the Black Hills, and climb as high as you can go, you'll find an area known as Hangman's Bluff. Not too long ago Zoroon's Castle faced a major uprising from the peasants in the countryside. Zoroon was a reasonable and respected leader. But his son and even more so his grandson were powermongers, bent on economic exploitation for personal gain. When the peasants could no longer tolerate the squalor and servitude which had ground them to near death, they took up arms and attacked the taskmasters and tribute collectors of Zoroon III. They were quickly suppressed and many were captured. A line of their emaciated forms stretched up the slopes of the tallest Black Hill bluff. On the top, they were hung, one after the other, for three days straight. Many watched. Most cried and the word went out about the intolerable injustice being done in this central Dregar province. It didn't take long for people from the city of Dresden and the Forest of Fog to rally to their cause. Zoroon III was overthrown soon after. The castle now stands nearly abandoned, certainly not the political figure it had once been.
Some residents of the central Dregar area trace the dark dirt and dimness of the Black Hills to this event. They argue that the hundreds of souls tortured and ripped from their body spread a pungent lament across the landscape. A few priests of Pranzis were recently sent to investigate this phenomenon. They didn't get far with the research, however, as they were run off by a camp of bugbears from the Eternal Flame clan. These elite agents of Bloodstone's evil machinations find the twisted and miserable conditions of the Black Hills quite welcoming. Since few people ever visit this woeful area, the bugbears were left to assemble numbers enough to best the Pranzis guards sent to deal with the situation.

Cave of the Snake
     The Cave of the Snake lies somewhere in the southern Serpent Mountains. Those few who have spelunked in this cave report that there are indeed large snakes in the depths. However, the upper layers are filled with Blood's Eternal Flame bugbears. There are reports of snake paintings on the walls of the upper levels and that the Eternal Flames, in any region, have shed snake skins wrapped around the handles of their weapons. This leads some bugbear experts to the conclusion that the Eternal Flame bugbears are a snake worshipping cult, and that this cave has central significance for their organization.

Corax Lake
    Every year, on the spring equinox, the people of Southern Dregar and the Pranzis area gather at Corax Lake for a festival. Joyous music and wild dancing ripple the surface of this unusually calm lake. People come in large groups to avoid the danger on the roads, quickly swelling the crowds at the lake to huge proportions. 
    The main event at the festival is the Corax Dive. When the Dive is about to begin, the crowd gathers around the lake and watches a small boat paddle out to the center. From the boat several long strands of woven rope with a large bright yellow rock tied to the end are lowered into the water. Along the rope are small detachable pouches of leather which are sealed off to float and suspend the rope. These pouches are painted particular colors at different lengths of the rope. The music changes from the festival tunes and resonates with the dangerous acts about to be performed. The divers then swim to the middle of the lake and when the whistle is blown their feet fly into the air and then disappear into the depths. The winner is the diver who can bring the deepest leather pouch to the surface.
    The excitement of the contest is heightened by the sheer depth of the lake. In some places, it is said, there is no bottom. Every few years one of the ropes goes missing, supposedly pulled by the yellow rock down into an eternal depth. The lake used to be called Deep Lake until Corax came along and stunned everyone with his diving ability. The half-orc barbarian dove swiftly to the bottom of one of the ropes and after an amazingly long time holding his breath emerged near the shore with the yellow rock rather than one of the leather pouches. The crowd was whipped into jubilation. After that day, people began to call the lake Corax Lake. In recent years the surveyors in Pranzis have made this name more official, giving the lake dual nomenclature.
    Corax's dive was hundreds of years ago. Since then no-one has come closer than 10 pouches away from the yellow stone. This fact has made people grow increasingly suspicious about Corax's feat and the nature of the lake.

Dalos Lake
    Dalos Lake is named for a mid-kingdom prince who used to daydream here. He spent such an inordinate amount of time at the banks of its calm and soothing waters that his father sent spies to monitor his activities there. That same trip, a giant snatched up the prince into his huge arms and lumbered away faster than they could follow. When the king learned of this he sent a brigade of his finest after his son's kidnapper. Many giants died in the pursuit and a few horsemen fell as well. When they reached the cave where his son was, they attacked the giant before surveying the situation. Nearly all involved died:  most of the brigade, over 50 giants, the son, and the kidnapping giant. With his cracked skull held in the firm arms of a Pranzis guard, the prince whispered that the giant was a friend, not a kidnapper, and he cursed his father for his meddling. 
    In commemoration of the wicked event, the king and the giant's ruler agreed to designate Dalos Lake as neutral ground. No skirmishes should be fought there between the giants and the Pranzis guards, but often are anyway. Beyond the lake the two great powers clash with fervent hatred and a skewed battle cry, both of which are rooted in that fateful series of events.

Dark Forest
    The Dark Forest is naturally dark. Black oaks create much of the dense canopy and the soil is a rich brown color. As if drawn by the name of this forest, a few hundred years ago something turned the essence of this forest figuratively dark as well. Many adventurers have sought the cause of this darkness, but they have only ever found its effects. These effects include dark spiders and dark treants, locally twisted and powerful varieties of spiders and treants. Rumors abound of a particularly deadly spider deep in the swamps at the northern rim of the forest. The forest has also become overrun by black snakes and shadow trolls, who have established some sort of complex organization and cave system just south of the forest.
    Those who have studied the forest believe that the whole area was cursed by an evil cleric long ago. Some believe that it happened while the drow concealed themselves in these forests to launch attacks upon Pranzis. They used the dense tree cover and unnatural darkness to conceal their dark deeds and shade their red eyes. Others think the timing is off, and that the forest was tainted a few decades before the drow arrived. They suggest that there is some unholy force which continues to flow into the River of Shadows and is then absorbed into the dark soil. The likely source of this unholy contamination is the crypts which are concealed by the dense forest growth. None, however, have delved more than a few hundred yards into the overwhelmingly evil Mosscrypt, so named for its mossy opening and entryway.

Darkland Mountains
    The Darkland Mountains to the north of the Great Rift seem to siphon some of its negative energy into the area, absorbing it into the unsettled earth. Things seem to change quickly and radically in the Darkland Mountains, as if some great force rearranges the whole range every day. This, of course, makes it impossible to have predictable routes through the range and makes it easy to get lost and cornered. The changes may be due to the forces from the Great Rift themselves, or they may be wrought at the hands of the Great Rift Giants who have migrated to this area. These massive and powerful creatures have been seen carrying boulders the size of houses. They may indeed have the collective strength to move the whole mountain, as it is suggested they do. Still, what purpose they have in doing so remains another of Dregar's great mysteries.

Deadman's Pass
    Deadman's Pass is the only road through the central ranges of Dregar if you are not on foot and well prepared. The pass separates the Spine and Serpent Mountains. At one point Pranzis protected the pass with intense vigilance. Deadman's Pass is the place that the "True Line," that started with Raklin Loenar as first Emperor in Pranzis, ended. The fifth ruler in that family line was slain by a guard that protected him in this pass, and to this day you can still see his grave.
    Now, however, since the Dark Forest just west of the pass has grown even darker and fewer people use the pass for legitimate travel, Pranzis has let its vigilance slip. Every once in a while you can hear someone in the capital crying out from the steps or a crate about what should be done about this crucial road. They have a point, as scouts have reported that the powerful forces of Blood have set up camp there and perform aggressive fundraising for their evil cause. "Didn't we learn anything from the Drow attacks?  A whole army can come through that pass and down through the Dark Forest!" The paranoid crier's warning spreads throughout the city, but the King's attention seems drawn elsewhere.

Drift Lands-Anuroch Desert
    The rain shadow of the Spine Mountains creates this expansive desert. It is so expansive that those desert druids and oasis dwellers have distinguished between three desert zones. There is the high mesa region, which is home to the Oasis giants. There is the deep valley desert in the northern areas, where scorpions and vipers are said to roam. There are also the dunes and sandstorm deserts, which are whipped into their wild forms by the eastern coastal gusts. There you can find armies of ants and formians, creatures whose sturdy exoskeletons protect them from the blasting sandstorms. These creatures have dwelled in the desert as long as anyone can remember. Their presence is simply natural for those who live in the Drift Lands.
    This desert is nicknamed the Drift Lands for one reason: huge sections of the desert seem to drift around. When they drift, they pull open great chasms and cause deep sinkholes. The shifting and churning desert has swallowed whole villages. The tips of their ruined abodes reach out from the sand as if in a last gasp for recognition. There are a few stable areas, though predictably, they tend to be home for the desert dwellers mentioned above and thus are the most dangerous.

Drift Lands Caves
    Beneath the Anuroch Desert are the Drift Lands Caves. These caves stretch in all directions underneath the great desert. Some believe the caves even open up in the Spine Mountains and Forest of Fog, but those routes are unlikely to be found and impossible to remain, because the same churning which pulls the desert around in maddening directions is also what gives form to these caverns. New caverns open and old ones fold in on themselves every day. This makes the Drift Lands Caves a risky but exciting venture for many dwarves and gnomes who seek the mineral treasures uncovered by the churning caverns.
Some treasure hunters also seek the great lost city of Anuroch. This city, the jewel of Dregar in the years before the great Cataclysm, is said to have fallen deep into the earth when the Cataclysm tore the desert into the huge chunks which slide around today. Treasure hunters boast that the vaults of this ancient city would hold riches beyond belief, and whoever finds them will surely be wealthy - and famous - all the days of her or his life.
    Only the mad or ridiculously brave will even set one foot into these caves to attempt to find the treasure or chip a few minerals. Oasis Giants block almost every stable passage in these caverns. And if those who delve deep enough, like few fateful parties have done, encounter one of Layonara's most feared beasts. The locals call her the Long Storm, a dragon whose very sight sends most people into a heart wrenching panic. The Long Storm emerges from the desert cave to torment Saudiria and other hamlets near the desert from time to time. Mostly she bursts in a huge cloud of sand from the smooth desert floor right at the beginning of a great sand storm and desert quake. It is unknown whether she causes them or knows they are about to happen and leaves the earth temporarily for the safe yet exposed sky. Either demonstrates her awesome power.

Forest Giant Cave
    Within the Forest of Fog there is a cave which seems to serve as the central settlement of the Broken Glade Giants. Their chief lives with his elite guard and many other giants among the amazing natural vaults and stalagmites and stalactites that form great pillars. When Pranzis comes on their frequent giant raids, the Broken Gladers pull back into the caves and defend the entrance. With great might and amazing numbers, the Broken Gladers fight back the attack and then begin to plan, in the messy giant way, for their counter-raid on Pranzis and surrounding environs.

Forest of Fog
    One of the largest and oldest forests of Layonara, the Forest of Fog is also one of the most mysterious. It is said that more rangers and druids live in this forest than any other in Layonara. Despite this, Bloodstone's bugbears find footholds in the wooded valleys and barren bluffs, from which they strike out with their brutal raiding parties. The bugbears simply appear in the forest, despite the patrols established to track their movements and keep them out. 
    The Broken Glade giants live in these woods as well and they are no less a mystery than the suspicious movements of the bugbears. The giants lived in, and some argue tended, the forest for many years before Bloodstone's return. In recent years, however, the Broken Glade giants are being designated by officials in Pranzis as enemies and allies of Blood. These officials assert this forcefully and seem unwilling to entertain other reasoning about the giants, despite the attempts by a group of rangers to portray the situation differently. Conflict has increased and aggressive maneuvers by both the Broken Gladers and the Pranzis guard have been witnessed. The Rangers of the Glade, as they have come to be known, assert that the aggression on the part of the giants is a response to the actions of Pranzis. Pranzis, and most Dregarians, view the increased hostility as an effect of Blood's influence over these weak-minded behemoths.
    As for the forest itself, what makes it mysterious and spectacular are the unexplainable mists which sweep across the forest unpredictably and without warning. Many travelers have found themselves far off course when the thick layer of mist blanketed the forest floor. Every year some go missing, even those traveling together in the same caravan. Mothers, husbands, guards, or companions either wander wildly to their peril or are abducted somehow by the mist itself. Those who live in the forest have far less trouble as they know to wait the mist out or use the trees, which jut gracefully from the mist, as markers and guides. Occasionally, however, a ranger disappears as well.
    Many adventurers have sought the source of this mist. Some say it is a lake. Many argue it pours from the mouth of a cave. Others believe the mist is the breath of the trees or Katia herself.

Great Plains of Dregar
    Dregar's Great Plains stretch from the east to the west coast beneath the northern mountain ranges. Silt carried down from the mountain run-off makes the plains extraordinarily fertile. Those who live there, particularly in the rolling hills region, boast that the Great Plains of Dregar has the best soil and produce in all of Layonara. The plains are also subject to frequent flooding. Scholars have spent countless hours trying to apply a schedule to the flooding, but to no avail. To some this is a sign of malevolent machination; to others, it is a sign of nature's mystery.

Great Rift
    It seems like the land in this area was grabbed in both hands by a god and ripped apart, leaving a huge gouge and jagged landscape. Every step through the surface area of the rift is laborious and treacherous. The Great Rift Giants, which dwell on the plateaus on the surface and in surrounding areas, attack on sight. These giants are tall even among giants, and have displayed exceptional visual acuity in hunting the large grey-backed armadillos that superbly blend into the craggy grey rocks. Their height and sharp vision means they can see intruders coming a long way off. These giants, it is argued by scholars in Pranzis, are stone giants who have been transformed by the energy wafting out of the cracks in the violent landscape here. The Bloody Stump giants, as they are called for their unusual constitution, are able to withstand (and sometimes even regenerate limbs lost from) dismembering blows, and are regarded as a more intense version of their surface cousins.
    Besides all the chasms and cracks, there is also a cave opening somewhere in the Great Rift. No one knows for sure what creatures dwell in the unending depths of the Rift itself, but tales concoct the vilest creatures imaginable. Wafting from this cave mouth is an intense negative energy. It sweeps across and transforms the whole area. Few have stood at its opening and lived to tell about it. Those few who have, always returned somehow transformed, turned wicked. A royal survey crew, accompanied by the King's best knights, was lost at this cave opening. One of the knights was seen a few months later wearing jet black armor and singlehandedly sacking the whole town of North Fort. Since then, the Rift has been officially designated as off limits by the crown.     Those wishing to venture there are asked to speak to the King's advisors to establish a formal team.

Iron Hills
    The high iron content in the soil here gives the hills a brilliant red color. Children's stories of the region, however, attribute the red soil to the countless who have spilled blood in ogre raids. Needless to say, ogres are feared in the area. Since the local farmers stay far from the ogre cave in the Iron Hills, the ogres have, for the most part, let the farmers be.

O'Taogor
    Some of the mightiest trolls known in Layonara live in this cave system. It seems that they were drawn here by the expansive caverns and the underground lake. These Trolls are so fierce that those who have faced them insist that their power must have been gifted from Bloodstone or one of the evil gods. Their community seems nearly entirely underground and they seldom venture from the cave mouth. Despite this, many believe that the day will come when Blood or some other wicked force will whisk their masses into action. As such, the entrance along the River of Shadows is always under hidden surveillance and a system of messengers can relay an alarm quickly to Pranzis and nearby towns if the need arises.

River of Shadows
    This river either picks up its negative energy as it passes through the Dark Forest or is itself the source of that negative energy as its water is absorbed by the dark flora. In either case, the river draws dark creatures to it, whether in the forest or as it emerges from the forest and spills into the northernmost regions of the Southern Plains. Malar panthers, vampires, and black snakes all find the banks of this river a welcoming abode. There is also a temple of Baraeon Ca'Duz somewhere near one of the stagnant back-current pools. Those who know about this temple are up in arms about it. There have been many petitions to the king to do something about it and many Dregarians have tried to take matters into their own hands, with little success. Those who live near the Dark Forest blame the temple for the proliferation of the spiders which sneak into their village and steal away loved ones at night. The priests of the temple insist that they are just there to study and pay respects to the great spiders of the Black Forest region.

Rolling Hills
    The Rolling Hills are in the central region of the Great Dregar Plains. Even though they don't reach very high, they can be seen for miles around on the flat farmlands. The sudden rise of these gentle bluffs spawned all sorts of mythologies and gives the hills a spiritual presence in the lives of the nearby farmers. 
    Many halflings have settled in these comfortable hills. Recently, the human farmers down in the nearby farm plains have begun to call the halflings' land rights into question. The hills, according to the human agriculturalists, were left undeveloped for a specific reason. They were used as funerary mounds for many generations of their ancestors. As the halflings dig their homes into the hills, they claim, they are desecrating not simply graves and memories, but the connection each human farmer has with her and his ancestors. The halfing newcomers refuse to leave, claiming traditional halfling land-use customs. Dregar has sent mediators to the area to try to work something out. The talks are heated, but no violence has erupted between the two groups yet.

Serpent Mountains
    These mountains are named more for the treacherous, serpentine paths and poisonous plants than any overwhelming presence of snakes or serpent-like creatures. Reports from mountain scouts suggest that there are also bugbears holed up in many of the remote valleys. Despite these trials and dangers, the Serpent Mountains are simply sublime and draw nature lovers and adventurers throughout Layonara to behold the expansive vistas, gently tumbling waterfalls and myriad species of trees.

Singing Forest
    The amazing thing about the Singing Forest is that it actually does sing. Those residents of northern Dregar who can afford to often make treks to this forest for purposes of spiritual rejuvenation or respite from their arduous daily existence. It has long been a debate whether the gentle song of this sublime forest is magical or if it emerges out of the unplanned and un-conducted confluence of the various forest sounds. Scholars of Katia who argue the latter also believe that the forest here, because of this emergent symphonic organization, has taken on a kind of aggregate identity. In other words, many who have studied the forest say that it is alive and self-aware in a way unlike any other forest in Layonara. If you visit, expect to be asked to leave after a very short stay if you aren't willing to merge with the forest and surrender your autonomy to its supra-individual agency.
Within this forest there are ancient ruins. Some of them seem to crumble more rapidly under the sway of the forest's singing, while others seem almost animated by it. There is one ruin that somehow seems to manage both. Every once in a while a creature enters the forest and finds the singing to be hideous and piercing. They scramble about, searching frantically for a way to make the sound stop. When this happens, northerners say, they almost always find themselves at the entrance to one of the ancient ruins. And as they step through the threshold they are transformed and lost from sight. Because of this, northerners call them the Ruins of Madness and have long spread the word to avoid it at all costs.

Southern Plains
    These plains run between the west coast of Dregar and the Forest of Fog. Depending on who you ask, the whole southern tip of Dregar may be considered a part of these broad, windswept grasslands. For many years, these plains were wild and left uncivilized by the power of Pranzis, which was distracted by other dark deeds at the time. Since the horsemen rode though and established control at Lorindar, the plains have become uniquely peaceful and settled. Blood's armies seem to gather elsewhere and direct their attention to other targets. As this information spreads more and more people seem to be traveling south. Many new settlements have sprung up across the Southern Plains and the established cities in the plains are finding themselves faced with a population issue.

Spine Mountains
    The Spine Mountains are like the backbone of Dregar, jutting out from its earthy flesh as they run long-ways down the continent. Dregar mythology portrays these mountains as the spine of one of the original dragons who lay down in the ocean near the beginning of time to create the central region of Layonara. The tremors which send avalanches of snow and rock down upon the lower regions occasionally remind people of their indebtedness to this dragon. Those who actively assert this idea, rather than just live with it as a dead tradition, explain all of Dregar's natural and magical activity in terms of this dragon. They also believe that one day the dragon will shake the soil from its scales and rise into the heavens again. Then it will shrug off the arrogant non-believers to drown in the ocean while gathering the faithful to its bosom as it flies toward the stars.

Storm Horn Mountains
    As the name suggests, the Storm Horn mountains are thrashed nearly every day of the year with violent storms. Only the most resilient barbarians lived here for centuries. These barbarians, also known as scryers, eventually acclimated and adapted to their environment. One peculiar feature of these barbarians is their massive lungs and amplifying voice box. They are said to be able to hurl a battle cry through a thundering storm with far better range and force than any other barbarian standing on a sunny field.
    The Storm Horn barbarians, however, have not been seen in the Storm Horn Mountains for ages. It seems that they were forced from their homeland by an invasion of Bleeding Rock Giants supposedly delivered to the Strong Horn's door by none other than Sinthar Bloodstone. This, according to historians, is one of the first things Blood did when he returned, indicating either some crucial significance to the area or a grudge against these barbarians. Every Storm Horn, however, vows at the age of manhood to strive every day toward reclaiming their precious homeland. 

Triera Mountains and the Thunder Peaks
    There is much exposed granite in these areas. Stone giants who moved here ages ago build simple structures out of it. For many years these giants smashed and shaped the granite by hand. Either by some process of natural changes - or as a gift from Grannoch as the giants themselves claim - they have developed extraordinarily large hands with sharp knuckles that can strike a rock like the most powerful pick ever made by man or dwarf. A passing half Deep Grove giant observed these giants smashing whole granite shelves into crude blocks and was awestruck. Triera worked his way into the giant's community and began to show them how to be more precise with their stone smashing. Triera spent many years in the late 12th century selling these blocks to castles and cities throughout Dregar. He named these giants the Granite Fists and he was said to have badly exploited them. When his life drew towards its end, Triera felt remorse for this exploitation, the people of northern Dregar assert. Because of this he bought the whole range of mountains, which was really only a few parcels he didn't already own, and gifted it to the giants. 
    A recent fire in the Pranzis hall of records, however, has conveniently destroyed any documentation that the Granite Fists are the rightful owner of their granite ranges. No one really recognizes giants as true owners of land in Dregar anyway. Adventurous stonemasons now gingerly tread into the Triera mountains in search of good granite slabs to export to growing cities. Conflicts, as you might expect, have begun to flare, making this a particularly hot and contested region of Dregar. Many of the Granite Fists have now migrated to the neighboring Thunder Peaks.

Troll Mountain
    At one point in Dregar's history there were trolls throughout the northeastern region. Giants and encroaching human development pushed them far into the mountains, toward the coast. For ages they have lived there in nearly complete isolation. Because of this, they have become their own sub-species of troll. The mountain which most of them call home grants these trolls its nomenclature: they are called the Troll Mountain Trolls.
The ocean views from Troll Mountain are breathtaking. Word of Troll Mountain's snowy beauty has tumbled down the slope to nearby human settlements and explorers have begun to carve trails through the ranges to this rare coastal peak. As more and more explorers and winter wonderland seekers make their way to Troll Mountain, organizations bent on the eradication of the Troll Mountain Trolls become more populous and outspoken.
The stenciled letters beneath the stylized jhemina just reads "AL'S PLACE".
Though the gnarled wood bows and creaks under heavy weight, this makeshift ramp seems sturdy enough.

Amenithruila, a gentle elf who has been stationed in Hlint for as long as any can remember.  With nut brown hair and a wit that is as sharp as her nature is caring, her easy and outgoing disposition has earned her many friends among adventurers, the common folk and influential Hlintites alike.  Indeed it is even noted that the Captain of Hlint's Guard has winked at her on many occasions...the Ilsarian just pointedly looking the other way....

Taking over for her father as captain of the guard is Alicia Nefzen, who spent most of her younger years itching to join Garent on his patrols and weapons training. Though it took longer than many expected for the stubborn Garent to relinquish his duties, this sturdy warrior now keeps the peace her father and many others fought for within the growing town of Hlint.

This is a statue of the elven deity Ilsare, also known as The Gentle Binder, Insightful Dreamer, the Songstress, whose dogma is: Less constructed around onerous rules than other faiths, the laws handed down by Ilsare are at once very simple and rather complex.  The Gentle Binder does not confuse her clergy with abundant letters and laws. The only parchment scribed by her clergy being beautiful poems or scores for music.  One could however argue that messages are still found within, even if they are not straight forward law.

Ilsare has a rather simple purpose, and though the faith would tell there are many additions to the simplistic core of her dogma, in its unadorned nature easily translates to "Follow ones heart while doing only the best for the hearts of others."  This of course applies equally to artists and lovers, it being a given that gifted creators have the best interests of the art at heart, lovers each other.

Such a simple statement on the surface, yet to actually understand the desire and love contained within self, and then to follow the path that it sets forth is no an easy task.  Ilsare also expects that such understanding is gained in accord with the virtues of love that she expresses, as presented by her stars and festivals both.
